# Wagonways Before Steam

Railways began as a way of moving heavy loads over the ground with less effort, and for most of their early history they were a problem of friction rather than power. A cart on a dirt track must overcome the resistance of soft ground, ruts, and uneven wheels. A cart on a smooth, hard, level surface needs far less force to keep moving. The earliest wagonways exploited this simple physical fact, and they grew out of the mines and quarries of Europe, where the cost of hauling ore and coal was the difference between a profitable operation and a ruined one.

Wooden tracks guided wheeled carts in German mining districts by the sixteenth century. Georgius Agricola's *De Re Metallica*, published in 1556, describes and illustrates the methods of mining and metallurgy as they were practiced in central Europe, and its woodcuts show carts running on timber rails, pushed by workers or drawn by animals. The principle was that a flanged wheel or a guiding edge kept the vehicle on its line, while the smooth wooden surface reduced rolling resistance. Such tracks were cheap to lay in a mine or a pit, and they could be relaid as the workings moved. They were not ambitious, but they were practical, and they spread.

In Britain the same logic took hold in the coalfields of the north-east and in the industrial districts of the Midlands. The wagonways of the Tyne and Wear, serving the collieries around Newcastle, were among the most important. By the seventeenth century, coal was being carried from pit heads to the riverside staithes on wooden tracks, and horses pulled loaded wagons downhill to the river while they hauled empty ones back up. The gravity of the slope did much of the work, and it became common practice to let loaded wagons run under their own weight, with horses or men controlling the descent. Coal in those days was heavy, bulky, and cheap, so the cost of moving it was decisive, and a wagonway that halved the cost of transport could open up a colliery that had been too far from market to be worth working.

The wooden rails of these early lines wore out quickly under the loads placed upon them. Iron soon replaced wood, first as a plate or strip nailed to the timber to protect it, and later as a rail in its own right. Iron rails were stronger, lasted longer, and could carry heavier wagons. Cast iron was brittle, however, and the early iron rails, which were often cast in short lengths, were prone to breaking under impact. The great improvement came in the eighteenth century with the ironworks at Coalbrookdale in Shropshire. Abraham Darby and his successors, working with coke-smelted iron, produced cast iron on a scale that made iron rails practical, and in the 1760s and 1770s the Coalbrookdale works supplied rails for local tramways. The Shropshire district around Broseley and Ironbridge became one of the first places in which the iron railway was developed systematically.

The engineering of these wagonways was learned empirically. Builders discovered that a flanged wheel of the right diameter, running on a rail of the right profile, kept the vehicle on track and reduced the danger of derailment. They also discovered that the gauge, the distance between the rails, should be consistent along the whole line, since a vehicle could not run on a track that varied in width. The sense that a railway was a system of components, with the rails, the wheels, the vehicles, and the gradients all matched to one another, grew out of these practical experiences and was never fully abandoned.

The eighteenth century also saw the first wagonways that carried goods for hire rather than serving a single owner's works. The Middleton Railway near Leeds, which was authorized in 1758 and opened in the following decades, is often cited as the first railway in the modern sense, because it carried coal for a number of customers over a public line for a fee. The principle that a railway could be a common carrier, offering transport to all comers, was an important step. It pointed toward the public railway of the nineteenth century, in which the track was built by one body and the trains run by many.

The wagonways of this period were, in their way, an achievement of practical intelligence. Their builders were not theorists. They were colliery viewers, mining engineers, millwrights, and ironmasters, men who had to solve immediate problems of transport with the materials and skills at hand. Their knowledge accumulated quietly over two centuries, and by the end of the eighteenth century it had produced a technology that was ready to receive a new source of power. What the wagonway lacked was a motive force that did not depend on horses, men, or gravity alone. That force was about to arrive from a different branch of engineering.

# Steam Finds Its Rails

The steam engine was the device that made the railway possible as a means of transport rather than a means of local haulage. Its history before it reached the rails is itself a story of incremental improvement. Thomas Newcomen's atmospheric engine, first put to work in 1712, used steam condensed in a cylinder to draw a piston down by atmospheric pressure. It was enormously inefficient by later standards, consuming large quantities of coal, but it was reliable, and it was used for pumping water out of mines, where coal was abundant and cheap. Newcomen engines spread across the British and European coalfields in the first half of the eighteenth century.

James Watt's contribution, most famously the separate condenser patented in 1769, transformed the economics of the steam engine. By condensing steam in a vessel separate from the cylinder, Watt kept the cylinder hot and avoided the repeated heating and cooling that had wasted so much fuel. His later work on the double-acting engine, which applied steam to both sides of the piston, allowed the engine to produce rotary motion, and this made it suitable for driving machinery in mills and factories. Watt's engines were built by the firm of Boulton and Watt, and they were expensive, carefully controlled by their makers, and used mostly in stationary applications.

The idea of a steam carriage was older than any of these engines. Nicolas-Joseph Cugnot's steam tractor of the 1760s, built for the French army to haul artillery, is often cited as the first self-propelled road vehicle, but it was unstable and impractical. Steam carriages on roads were tried in Britain by Richard Trevithick, Goldsworthy Gurney, and others in the early nineteenth century, and they showed that a machine could move under its own power. The problem was that road surfaces were uneven, the machines were heavy, and the operators faced hostility from horse-drawn coach interests and turnpike trusts.

Richard Trevithick, a Cornish engineer, was the decisive figure in the transition to rail. Trevithick worked with high-pressure steam, which allowed a much smaller and lighter engine to produce a given power. Watt had been wary of high-pressure steam because the boilers of his day were not strong enough to contain it safely, and he worried about the risks of explosion. Trevithick developed boilers and engines that could operate at higher pressures, and in 1801 he built a steam road carriage that ran in Camborne, Cornwall. The following year he took out a patent for steam carriages and built a further vehicle that ran in London.

The first steam locomotive to run on rails was Trevithick's machine at the Penydarren ironworks near Merthyr Tydfil in South Wales. On 21 February 1804, it hauled a load of iron, reputedly about ten tons, together with a number of men riding on the wagons, along a tramroad of about nine miles. The journey was successful in the sense that the engine did what it was designed to do, but it was not a commercial triumph. The track could not bear the weight of the engine, which broke a number of the cast-iron rails, and the locomotive was soon taken out of service. Trevithick went on to build other locomotives, including the *Catch Me Who Can* in London in 1808, which ran on a circular track set up for public exhibition and attracted crowds, but he did not find a lasting business in building them. He was a restless inventor who moved from project to project, and he often sold his patents for little return.

The problem that defeated early locomotives was one of adhesion and track strength. A smooth wheel on a smooth rail slips, so that the engine turns its wheels without moving forward. Some early designers, including John Blenkinsop, tackled this by introducing a toothed rack on one rail, with a cogwheel on the locomotive engaging it. Blenkinsop's rack locomotive built for the Middleton Railway in 1812 was a working machine that hauled coal for some years, and it demonstrated that steam traction could be practical on a commercial line. Other engineers, notably William Hedley and Timothy Hackworth, built locomotives for the collieries of north-east England, including Hedley's *Puffing Billy* of 1813, and they experimented with smooth-wheeled machines that relied on the weight of the engine to provide grip.

George Stephenson was the engineer who brought these strands together into a locomotive that could serve a public railway. Working at the collieries around Newcastle, Stephenson built his first locomotive, *Blücher*, in 1814. It was a practical machine that could haul coal wagons, and it had a flanged wheel on a smooth rail, relying on adhesion rather than a rack. Stephenson went on to improve his locomotives through a series of designs, paying attention to the efficiency of the boiler, the layout of the cylinders, and the mechanism that connected them to the wheels. He was an engineer of the practical sort, a self-taught colliery mechanic who learned from trial and error, and his ability to combine engineering skill with a sense of the commercial possibilities of the railway made him the central figure of the early period.

The decisive demonstration came with the Stockton and Darlington Railway, which opened on 27 September 1825. The line had been promoted by Quakers and merchants of Darlington and was intended primarily to carry coal from the collieries of south-west Durham to the port of Stockton on the Tees. It was a public railway in the sense that it could be used by different owners, and Stephenson's *Locomotion No. 1* hauled the first train, which carried coal and a number of passengers. Some of the early traffic was horse-drawn, and the company used both horses and locomotives during the first years of operation. The Stockton and Darlington nonetheless demonstrated that steam locomotion could work on a line carrying real freight, and it established a model that other railways would follow.

# The Liverpool and Manchester and the Idea of the Railway

The Stockton and Darlington was a coal railway in the north-east, but the Liverpool and Manchester Railway, which opened on 15 September 1830, was something different. It connected two of the largest and fastest-growing commercial centres in Britain, and it was intended to carry passengers as well as cotton and other goods. Its promoters were merchants and manufacturers who had concluded that the canal system, which had served the region well, could not meet the growing demands of trade. The canal between the two cities was slow, the roads were congested and expensive, and the traffic between Liverpool, the port through which Lancashire's cotton arrived, and Manchester, the centre of its spinning and weaving, required something faster and more reliable.

The Liverpool and Manchester was therefore designed from the start as a showcase for the steam locomotive and a test of its commercial possibilities. Its directors held a competition in 1829 at Rainhill, near Liverpool, for locomotives that could meet a set of demanding conditions: a locomotive had to haul a specified load at a set speed over a fixed distance, and it had to be reliable, economical, and within a weight limit. Stephenson's *Rocket*, built with his son Robert and the assistance of Henry Booth, won the competition. The *Rocket* was not the only entry, and Timothy Hackworth's *Sans Pareil* and other engines took part, but *Rocket* combined several innovations, including a multitubular boiler that greatly increased the heating surface and therefore the production of steam, and a blast pipe that drew the exhaust steam up the chimney and quickened the draught through the fire. These features made it the template for the locomotives that followed.

The opening of the line was marked by a tragedy that the promoters had not intended. William Huskisson, the Member of Parliament for Liverpool and a former minister, had been invited to the ceremony. At the stop at Parkside, he left his carriage to speak with the Duke of Wellington, who was also present, and he was struck by the locomotive *Northumbrian* as it passed on the adjoining track. He died of his injuries that evening. His death was a shock to the public, and it was a sign that the railway would bring dangers as well as benefits. It also made the railway a matter of national attention, and the newspapers reported it widely.

The Liverpool and Manchester is significant for more than its technology. It demonstrated the possibility of a railway as an integrated system, with its own timetables, its own signals, its own staff, and its own management structure. The company had to solve problems that had not arisen on the colliery lines, including the organization of passenger services, the handling of goods at terminals, the division of responsibility between engineers and managers, and the relationship between the railway and the public. Its directors and engineers established practices that became standard across the railway world, and the line showed that a railway could make money by carrying passengers at a regular interval and at a reasonable fare.

The success of the Liverpool and Manchester had profound effects on public opinion. Before 1830, the railway was a curiosity, a tool for coal and iron. After 1830, it was recognized as a force that would reshape the economy. Investors saw the profits that could be made from passenger traffic, and engineers and entrepreneurs began to propose railways in every part of the country. The concept of a railway network, in which lines would be joined together to form a system, began to appear in the proposals of the 1830s. The railway was no longer a local expedient. It was a national project.

The line also shaped the professional identity of the railway engineer. Robert Stephenson, who became one of the most eminent engineers of the nineteenth century, learned his craft in the field and in the drawing office, and he carried the methods of the colliery engineer into the design of the main-line railway. Isambard Kingdom Brunel, who came to the railway from a background in civil engineering and architecture, brought a different sensibility, emphasizing the grand scale and the aesthetic quality of the work. Between them, these engineers defined the profession that would build the railways of the next half century.

# The Railway Mania and the Shaping of a Network

The years from the mid-1830s to the late 1840s saw a rush of railway promotion in Britain that has been called the Railway Mania. The term describes both the enthusiasm of investors and the speculation that accompanied it. Railway companies were founded in great numbers, each one seeking an Act of Parliament to authorize its construction, each one issuing shares to finance the work, and each one promising returns that were often exaggerated. The mania reached its peak in 1845 and 1846, when Parliament received proposals for thousands of miles of new line, and when share prices rose and fell in a cycle of hope and disappointment.

The mania was driven by genuine economic reasons as well as by speculation. Railways offered a fast and cheap means of moving goods and people, and they promised to connect regional markets that had been isolated by the difficulties of road transport. Investors who had made money in canals and turnpikes saw the railway as the next stage of transport investment, and merchants who had long complained about the cost of carriage saw in the railway a means of reducing it. Many of the proposed lines were sensible, and a large number were eventually built. Many others were badly conceived, duplicated existing routes, or were simply paper schemes that never saw a rail laid.

Parliament played a central role in the mania. Each railway had to pass through a private Act, a process that involved examination by committees, the hearing of evidence from landowners and other interested parties, and the negotiation of compromises. The process was slow and expensive, and it gave a great deal of influence to the railway promoters who could afford to pay the parliamentary agents and the lawyers. Parliament also decided the routes of many lines, which meant that the political and social interests of the landowning class and of the towns affected the shape of the network.

The mania led to the creation of many of the great railway companies that would dominate the British railway system until nationalization. The London and North Western, the Great Western, the Midland, the Great Northern, the Lancashire and Yorkshire, and others were built or consolidated during this period. Some of them were the result of mergers, in which companies absorbed their rivals and extended their networks. The process of amalgamation was messy and sometimes bitter, and it created a set of large regional companies that competed fiercely for traffic.

The Railway Mania ended in a financial crash. Share prices collapsed in 1846 and 1847, many promoters were ruined, and the economy suffered a severe downturn. Several railway companies could not raise the capital to complete their works, and some abandoned their projects. The crash was a painful lesson, but it did not stop the growth of the railway. The lines that were built during the mania remained, and the railway network that resulted was the foundation of Britain's railway system for more than a century. By 1850, Britain had several thousand miles of railway, and the network radiated from London to the major cities of England, Scotland, and Wales.

The London termini of these railways were among the most striking features of the new system. Stations such as Euston, King's Cross, Paddington, and Liverpool Street were built as monuments to the railway companies, and their architecture reflected the pride and ambition of their owners. The termini were also a practical necessity, since each railway needed a place in the capital to receive its passengers and goods, and the construction of these stations involved the demolition of entire neighbourhoods. Over the following decades, the termini became the focal points of London's transport system, and their location shaped the growth of the city.

The mania also brought a change in the organization of the railway industry itself. Railway companies became large employers, with thousands of staff engaged in operating trains, maintaining track, managing stations, and handling freight. They developed hierarchical structures, with managers, engineers, clerks, and workers organized into departments. They also developed the practices of timetabling, signalling, and accounting that would become standard. The railway was one of the first industries in which large-scale management was necessary, and the methods devised in the 1840s and 1850s influenced the development of business organization more widely.

# Gauge, Regulation, and the Question of Standards

The railway had to solve the problem of standards, and this was one of the most contentious issues of the 1840s. The gauge, the distance between the inside faces of the rails, was not fixed. Stephenson's railways used a gauge of four feet eight and a half inches, a width that derived, by a long chain of tradition, from the wagonways of the north-east coalfield, which in turn had taken their width from the carts and the ruts of the roads. Brunel, however, built the Great Western Railway to a broad gauge of seven feet and a quarter inch. He believed that a wider gauge would allow greater stability, higher speeds, and a more comfortable ride, and he designed his locomotives and carriages accordingly.

The gauge question became a dispute of national importance. The Great Western and the standard-gauge companies competed for traffic, and where their lines met, passengers and goods had to be transferred from one gauge to another. This was slow, expensive, and inconvenient, and it imposed a real cost on the economy. The dispute was argued in the press, in Parliament, and among engineers, with partisans of each gauge claiming technical superiority for their preferred width. A Royal Commission was appointed in 1845 to examine the question, and its report led to the Gauge Act of 1846, which established the standard gauge of four feet eight and a half inches as the required width for most new lines. The broad gauge survived on the Great Western and a few other lines for decades, and it was finally abolished in 1892, when the last broad-gauge track was converted.

The Gauge Act is an example of the way that the railway forced the state to take an interest in technical standards. Before the railway, transport had been regulated mainly by local authorities and by the owners of turnpikes, canals, and roads. The railway, by contrast, required a national framework, since its lines were interconnected and its traffic crossed boundaries. Parliament had to decide not only who could build railways but how they should be built, and the Gauge Act was a significant step in that direction.

Another important early intervention was the Railway Regulation Act of 1844, which was associated with the name of William Ewart Gladstone, then President of the Board of Trade. The Act required railway companies to provide cheap third-class passenger trains, at a fare of a penny a mile, on certain lines, and it set minimum standards for the safety and comfort of third-class carriages. It also gave the state the right to purchase railways after a set period, and it created a system of inspection by officers of the Board of Trade. These provisions reflected a concern that the railways, if left entirely to private enterprise, would neglect the needs of the poorer travellers and would endanger the public.

The Act of 1844 established a pattern that continued throughout the nineteenth century, in which the state intervened to regulate the railway in the interests of the public while leaving the ownership and management of the lines largely in private hands. Inspectors of railways, reporting to the Board of Trade, examined the design and operation of new lines, and they had the power to order improvements. Their reports were an important source of information about the safety of the system, and they helped to create a body of knowledge about accidents and their causes.

Accidents were a constant feature of the early railway, and the state's response to them shaped the development of safety practices. Collisions, derailments, and boiler explosions killed and injured many people. The introduction of the block system, in which the line was divided into sections and only one train was permitted in each section at a time, reduced the number of collisions on busy lines. The telegraph, which spread along the railways from the 1840s, allowed signalmen to communicate with each other, and it became essential to the safe working of the line. The development of continuous brakes, which applied braking force to every vehicle in a train from the engine, was slower, and it did not become universal until the later decades of the century.

The creation of the Railway Clearing House in 1842 was another step in the development of a national railway system. The Clearing House was established by the railway companies to settle the accounts for traffic that passed from one company's network to another. It allowed through tickets and through freight to be sold and carried over several railways, and it required agreements on tariffs, rolling-stock use, and the sharing of revenues. The Clearing House was a voluntary organization, but it became one of the most important institutions of the railway age, and it showed that the companies could cooperate when they had a common interest in doing so.

The problem of standards and regulation foreshadowed later debates about the railway as a public utility. The railway was a natural monopoly in many of its functions, since it was expensive to build a second line along the same route, and it was therefore tempting to see the state as the natural owner of the railway or as its regulator. Over the next century, the British government moved between laissez-faire, state regulation, and eventually nationalization. These debates had their origins in the period of the Railway Mania, when the public first began to see the railway as a matter of national concern.

# Crossing the Channel and the Continent

The railway came to continental Europe in the late 1820s and 1830s, and its introduction was shaped by the local conditions of each country. In France, the first railway was the line from Saint-Étienne to Andrézieux, a coal railway in the Loire district that was built in the late 1820s and used horses for much of its traffic. It was a modest line, but it attracted the interest of French engineers and entrepreneurs, who had been studying the British railways and who were eager to build their own. The French government and the engineers of the Corps des Mines and the Corps des Ponts et Chaussées took a keen interest in the new technology, and they sent a number of missions to Britain to study the lines and the locomotives.

Belgium was the first continental country to build a railway as a national project. The Belgian government, which had gained independence in 1830, decided that a railway network would bind the young state together and would give Belgian industry access to markets. The line from Brussels to Mechelen opened in 1835 and was the first intercity railway on the Continent. Belgium adopted the standard gauge, and the government took a direct interest in building and operating the railway, a model that influenced other countries. The Belgian railway was a state enterprise, and its success helped to establish the view that railways were a public responsibility and a tool of national policy.

Germany's first railway, the Ludwigsbahn between Nuremberg and Fürth, opened on 7 December 1835. It was a short line, about six kilometres long, and it was built by a private company with financing from Nuremberg merchants and bankers. The locomotive *Adler*, built in England, was the first steam locomotive to run in Germany, and the line carried passengers on a route that had previously been served by horses and coaches. Germany was then a patchwork of states, and the railway had to cross the frontiers of these states, which created complications over tariffs, gauges, and regulations. The development of the German railway network was therefore slower than that of Belgium, and it was closely tied to the process of political unification that culminated in the foundation of the German Empire in 1871.

Austria built its first major railway, the Kaiser Ferdinands-Nordbahn, which connected Vienna with the towns of Moravia and Bohemia, in the 1830s and 1840s. The line was financed by the Rothschild family and by other investors, and it carried coal and goods from the industrial districts of the north to the capital. Austria's mountainous terrain and its complex political structure made railway building especially difficult, and the Austrian railways developed a distinctive engineering tradition, most visible in the Semmering line of the 1850s, which will be discussed later.

The Russian Empire built its first railway from St Petersburg to Tsarskoye Selo, the imperial summer residence, which opened in 1837. The line was a showpiece, intended to demonstrate the power and modernity of the Tsarist state, and it was built by British engineers and with British locomotives. Russia's vast distances and its sparse population meant that railways would be slow to spread, but the government eventually built a network that would connect the empire's European and Asian territories. The Trans-Siberian Railway, begun in the 1890s and completed in 1916, was the greatest of these projects, and it is discussed below.

The continental railways shared a set of technical and political problems. Their engineers were trained in the French tradition of civil engineering, which emphasized mathematics, the theory of structures, and the design of large public works. The École Polytechnique and the École des Ponts et Chaussées produced engineers who designed the railways of France and of much of Europe. Their approach differed from that of the British engineers, who had come up through the colliery and the workshop, and who had learned by doing. The continental railways were often built with more careful surveys and more elaborate structures, and they reflected the view that railways were public works of national importance.

Continental railways also developed their own locomotive designs. French engineers built locomotives with particular characteristics, and German engineers developed the Crampton locomotive, which had a large driving wheel at the rear and was favoured for fast passenger service on some lines. Locomotive builders in Germany, such as Borsig in Berlin, grew from small workshops into major manufacturers, and they supplied the railways of the German states and of other countries. By the middle of the century, the continental railway industry had become an important part of the European engineering sector, and it could compete with the British builders in both quality and price.

The continental railways were also shaped by strategic considerations. Governments saw the railway as a means of moving troops and supplies, and they took account of military needs in the planning of routes. The railway was used in the wars of the mid-nineteenth century, including the Crimean War and the wars of Italian and German unification, and the use of railways for military purposes became a central part of the strategy of the great powers. The Prussian army's ability to mobilize quickly by rail in 1866 and 1870 was one of the decisive factors in its victories, and it gave the railway a reputation as an instrument of state power.

By the 1850s, the railways of Europe had created a continental network that linked the major cities of the Continent. The distances were short compared to those of North America, and the networks were dense, with many lines crossing national boundaries and requiring agreements on tariffs, operations, and the interchange of rolling stock. The railway therefore became one of the earliest examples of a transnational technical system, in which the cooperation of states and companies was necessary for it to work. This cooperation was never simple, but it laid the groundwork for the international railway agreements of later decades.

# The American Railroad

The railway in the United States developed along lines that were in some respects similar to those in Britain and in others radically different. The American railroad was built in a country of vast distances, a sparse population, and abundant land, and its growth was shaped by the desire to open the interior of the continent to settlement and commerce. The first American railways were short lines connecting ports and cities on the Atlantic seaboard, and their builders were often merchants and civic leaders who hoped to draw trade from rival cities. The early lines were built with capital from local investors, and they were frequently financed by the sale of bonds and shares.

The Delaware and Hudson's Stourbridge Lion, imported from England in 1829, was the first steam locomotive to run on an American railroad, and it was used on a line in the coal districts of Pennsylvania. It was a British locomotive, built in the Stourbridge district, and it was too heavy for the track that had been laid, so it was used only briefly. Its significance lies in what it started. American engineers soon began building their own locomotives, and the American locomotive industry became a major force in the development of the railway. The Baltimore and Ohio Railroad, chartered in 1827, was the most important early American line. It was intended to connect the port of Baltimore with the Ohio River and to challenge the dominance of the Erie Canal in the trade of the interior.

The Baltimore and Ohio's engineers experimented with horses, sails, and steam. Peter Cooper, an inventor and industrialist, built a small locomotive called *Tom Thumb* in 1830 and ran it on the line, where it famously raced a horse-drawn car and lost when its drive belt slipped. The race was a publicity event, but it was also a demonstration of the problems of early American locomotive design. The line was soon using larger and more reliable locomotives, and by the 1840s it was operating a network that stretched westward toward the Ohio River.

American railroads developed a number of distinctive features that reflected the conditions of their country. The American locomotive was designed for the light and irregular track of the early lines, and the four-wheeled leading truck, which allowed the locomotive to negotiate curves, was developed to suit the sharp bends and poorly laid track of the American frontier. The cowcatcher, a device attached to the front of the locomotive to clear obstacles from the track, was a characteristic American invention, and it became an enduring symbol of the railroad. The American railway also used wood as fuel for much of the nineteenth century, because wood was cheap and plentiful, and the locomotives had large chimneys and spark arresters to reduce the risk of fires.

The railway of the United States was also shaped by the government's policy of land grants. The federal government and the states gave railway companies large tracts of public land along the routes of their lines, which the companies could sell to settlers to raise money for construction. The land grants made possible the construction of many lines that would otherwise have been uneconomic, and they encouraged the settlement of the Great Plains and the West. The grants were controversial, and they led to fraud, speculation, and the concentration of land in the hands of railroad companies. Nonetheless, they were a critical element of the transcontinental railroad.

The Pacific Railway Act of 1862, passed during the Civil War, authorized the construction of a railway between the Missouri River and the Pacific coast. Two companies were chosen to build the line, the Central Pacific from Sacramento, California, eastward, and the Union Pacific from Omaha, Nebraska, westward. The companies were financed by a combination of government bonds, land grants, and private capital, and they employed thousands of workers, many of them Chinese immigrants on the Central Pacific and Irish and other immigrants on the Union Pacific. The work was extremely dangerous, requiring the blasting of tunnels through the Sierra Nevada and the laying of track across the desert and the plains.

The two lines met at Promontory Summit in Utah on 10 May 1869, where a ceremonial golden spike was driven to mark the completion of the transcontinental railroad. The event was widely reported, and it was celebrated as a triumph of American enterprise and technology. The completion of the line made it possible to travel from the Atlantic to the Pacific in days rather than months, and it opened the western territories to settlement and commerce on a new scale. It also accelerated the destruction of Native American societies in the West and the expansion of American power across the continent.

The transcontinental railroad was followed by a wave of railway building that continued into the early twentieth century. Railway companies expanded rapidly, competing for traffic and territory, and they built lines across the Midwest, the South, and the West. The rivalry of the railroads led to ruinous rate wars, in which companies cut their prices to win traffic, and to a bitter struggle for control of the most profitable lines. Financiers such as Jay Gould, Cornelius Vanderbilt, and James J. Hill built railroad empires, and the railroad became the centre of American capitalism in the late nineteenth century.

The American railway also produced important technical innovations. George Westinghouse developed the air brake, which used compressed air to apply the brakes on every car of a train at once, and he patented it in 1869. The air brake was a major step in railway safety, since it allowed a train to be stopped quickly and reliably. The automatic coupler, patented by Eli Janney in 1873, replaced the dangerous practice of coupling cars by hand, which had maimed and killed many brakemen. George Pullman built sleeping cars that offered passengers comfortable overnight travel, and his company became one of the largest manufacturers of railway vehicles in the country.

The American railway also faced significant regulatory problems. Rate discrimination, in which companies charged different prices to different shippers and to different places, provoked protest from farmers and merchants, and it led to demands for government regulation. The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 established the Interstate Commerce Commission, the first federal regulatory agency in the United States, and it gave the government the power to oversee railroad rates and practices. The act was an important step in the development of American regulation, although the commission's powers were initially limited and were expanded only gradually over the following decades.

Labour conflict was a constant feature of the American railway. The railroad workers' unions, such as the Brotherhood of Locomotive Engineers and the Brotherhood of Railroad Trainmen, organized their members to demand better wages and conditions. The strikes of 1877, which spread across much of the country, and the Pullman strike of 1894, which was broken by federal troops and an injunction, were among the most dramatic episodes in the history of American labour. These conflicts shaped the politics of the Gilded Age and the development of the American state.

# Railways Across Empires and Oceans

The railway spread beyond Europe and North America in the second half of the nineteenth century, carried by the expansion of colonial empires, the investment of European capital, and the ambitions of non-European states. In many places, the railway was built by foreign engineers and financed by foreign investors, and it was intended to serve the economic interests of the colonial power or of the investing country. In other places, the railway was adopted by local rulers and governments who saw it as a means of modernization and of strengthening their state. The result was a global network of railways, uneven in its distribution and complex in its meaning.

In India, the railway was introduced in the 1850s under the auspices of the British East India Company, which had been persuaded by its directors and by the British government that railways would improve the administration of the subcontinent, facilitate the movement of troops, and promote the export of cotton and other raw materials. The first line, from Bori Bunder in Bombay to Thane, opened on 16 April 1853, and it was followed by lines connecting Calcutta, Madras, and other cities. The Indian railway was built largely with British capital, and it was operated by private companies under guarantees from the government. Its networks were designed to serve the economic interests of Britain and the administrative needs of the Raj, and they had profound effects on the social and economic life of the subcontinent.

The Indian railway was also a major employer and a vehicle for the movement of people. The railway carried pilgrims, migrants, soldiers, and traders across the country, and it helped to spread ideas and goods. It also contributed to famines, since railways could move food to some places but also could carry grain away from areas where it was needed, and the railway's relationship with agriculture and with the famine policy of the colonial government has been debated by historians. The railway was therefore both a tool of colonial exploitation and a means of social change, and its history in India is complex.

Japan's railway history began in 1872, when the line from Shimbashi in Tokyo to Yokohama opened, with British engineers and British locomotives. The Meiji government had decided to build railways as part of its program of modernization, and it entrusted the early lines to British advisers and contractors. The Japanese railway was rapidly expanded, and by the end of the century the country had a national network of lines, many of them built and operated by the state. The railway was a central element of Japan's industrialization and of its military strength, and it played a role in the country's expansion into Korea and Manchuria. The Japanese example demonstrated that a non-European country could build a modern railway system with foreign assistance and then take over the technology for itself.

China's railway history was more fraught. The first railway in China, the Wusong Railway, was built by a British company in 1876, connecting Shanghai with the town of Wusong. The line was controversial, and it was bought by the Chinese government and dismantled within a year, its equipment shipped away. The Chinese imperial government was suspicious of railways, which it associated with foreign influence and with the disruption of traditional society and economies. The railway came to China in earnest only in the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, when foreign powers obtained concessions to build lines in their spheres of influence, and when the Chinese government began to build its own railways. The conflict between foreign and domestic control of the railways played a part in the revolutionary movements of the early twentieth century.

Latin America saw the railway spread in the 1850s and later, with British, French, and American investors financing lines to connect ports with mining and agricultural regions. The Buenos Aires and Floresta railway, which opened in 1857, was one of the first in Argentina, and the Argentine railway expanded rapidly, linking the pampas with the port of Buenos Aires and making the country a major exporter of grain and meat. In Brazil, Mexico, Chile, and other countries, railways were built to serve export economies, and they reinforced the pattern of economic dependence on the industrialized countries. The Andes posed enormous engineering challenges, and some of the most dramatic lines in the world were built through the mountains of Peru, Bolivia, and Chile.

Australia and New Zealand built their railways in the 1850s and later. The Melbourne and Hobsons Bay Railway, which opened in 1854, was the first in Australia, and it was followed by lines in New South Wales, Queensland, South Australia, and Western Australia. The Australian colonies built their railways independently, and they adopted different gauges, a fact that created problems for the national network that were not solved until the twentieth century. The railways were built to serve mining, agriculture, and the movement of people and goods across the vast continent, and they played a central role in the development of the Australian economy.

Africa saw railways built in the late nineteenth century, primarily for colonial purposes. The railway from Alexandria to Cairo, begun in the 1850s, was one of the earliest in Egypt, and the Suez Canal was built during the same period. The colonial powers built railways to connect ports with mines and plantations, and to move troops and administrators. The Cape Government Railways in South Africa expanded rapidly after the discovery of diamonds and gold, and the Benguela Railway in Angola and the Uganda Railway in East Africa were built to link interior regions with the coast. The African railway was often built with forced labour or with labour recruited under harsh conditions, and its history is one of exploitation as well as of development.

The Trans-Siberian Railway was the greatest of the imperial projects of the late nineteenth century. Its construction was begun in 1891 under the direction of the Russian government, and it was intended to connect Moscow with Vladivostok on the Pacific coast, a distance of more than nine thousand kilometres. The line was built across the Ural Mountains, the Siberian plains, and the mountains and forests of the Far East, and its construction took more than two decades. The railway was completed in 1916, in the midst of the First World War, and it became one of the longest railways in the world. It transformed the economy of Siberia, opened the region to settlement, and gave Russia a means of projecting its power in East Asia.

The spread of the railway across the world was a process of enormous complexity. It brought new forms of wealth and new forms of dependence, new connections between regions and new barriers between them. It shaped the economies, politics, and cultures of the societies it touched, and it created new kinds of work and new kinds of community. Its history cannot be told as a simple story of progress, but it was one of the most powerful forces of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.

# Engineering the Impossible: Mountains, Tunnels, Bridges

The railway forced engineers to solve problems of terrain that had never before been encountered on such a scale. Roads could wind around hills, and canals could follow the contours of the land, but the railway required relatively level and direct routes, with gradients that a locomotive could climb and a train could hold back when descending. Railway engineers therefore had to cut through hills, fill valleys, build bridges across rivers and gorges, and tunnel through mountains. These works were among the most ambitious engineering projects of the nineteenth century, and they demanded new techniques of surveying, construction, and materials science.

The Semmering line in Austria, completed in 1854, was one of the first major mountain railways in Europe. Carl von Ghega, the engineer responsible for the project, designed the line to cross the Semmering Pass, a mountain barrier in the Alps between Vienna and the south. The line used a series of tunnels, viaducts, and curves to achieve a maximum gradient that locomotives of the time could manage, and it was an astonishing feat of engineering. Ghega's bridges, built of stone with elegant arches, were both practical and beautiful, and they became models for later mountain railways. The line was built under extremely difficult conditions, and it demonstrated that a railway could cross a high mountain range.

The Alpine railways that followed the Semmering included the Mont Cenis line, the Gotthard line, and the Brenner line, each of which faced its own challenges. The Mont Cenis Tunnel, begun in 1857 and completed in 1871, was one of the longest tunnels in the world at the time, running for more than twelve kilometres through the Alps between France and Italy. Its construction used compressed-air drills, which were among the first practical rock drills to be powered by compressed air, and the tunnel was bored from both ends. The Gotthard Tunnel, completed in 1882, was even longer and was the first Alpine tunnel to link northern and southern Europe through a single route. Its construction was financed by Swiss, German, and Italian investors, and it was one of the first major railway projects in which the cooperation of several nations was necessary.

The Gotthard line also used switchbacks and spiral tunnels to climb the steep approaches to the mountain. The spiral tunnels at Wassen, which loop under the valley to gain height, are a visible sign of the ingenuity required to build the line. The Gotthard was an enormous project, and it demonstrated that a railway could be built through the most difficult mountain terrain with the tools of the nineteenth century. A later and much longer tunnel, the Gotthard Base Tunnel, was opened in 2016. It runs for about fifty-seven kilometres through the Alps, and it allows trains to pass through the mountain at a relatively low altitude, avoiding the steep gradients of the old line. It is the longest railway tunnel in the world.

Rack railways were developed to climb gradients that were too steep for adhesion railways. The Mont Cenis Fell system, built in the 1860s, used a central rail between the running rails, which was gripped by horizontal wheels on the locomotive, allowing the engine to climb steep slopes. The Mount Washington Cog Railway, opened in New Hampshire in 1869, used a similar cog and rack system to reach the summit of one of the highest mountains in the northeastern United States. These railways were limited in their application, but they were essential for reaching mountain peaks and steep passes, and they are still operated today as tourist attractions and as working lines.

Tunnels under water posed special challenges. The Severn Tunnel, which runs beneath the Severn estuary between England and Wales, was opened in 1886 after more than a decade of construction. It was one of the longest underwater tunnels of its time, and its construction required the management of water seepage and the handling of pressures that threatened to flood the workings. The Channel Tunnel, which connects England and France beneath the English Channel, was opened in 1994 after many decades of planning. Its construction used tunnel boring machines to excavate the rock, and it required sophisticated engineering to keep the tunnels safe and dry. The Channel Tunnel allowed the Eurostar high-speed trains to run between London and Paris and Brussels, and it transformed the connection between Britain and the Continent.

Bridges were equally important to the railway. The Britannia Bridge, designed by Robert Stephenson and opened in 1850, crossed the Menai Strait between Wales and the island of Anglesey. It used tubular iron girders, through which trains passed, and it was one of the most innovative structures of its time. The bridge was damaged by fire in 1970 and was rebuilt with an arch above the girders. The Forth Bridge, opened in 1890, crossed the Firth of Forth in Scotland and used a cantilever design with massive steel structures. It was one of the first major bridges to use steel on a large scale, and it became an icon of Scottish engineering. Its construction required the work of thousands of men, and its design influenced the development of bridge engineering around the world.

Viaducts were another characteristic feature of the railway. The Göltzsch Viaduct in Germany, completed in 1851, is one of the largest brick structures in the world, with more than ninety arches carrying the railway over the Göltzsch valley. The viaducts of the railway were built in stone, brick, iron, and later steel, and they reflected the availability of materials and the skill of local masons and builders. They were often among the most visible and admired structures of the railway, and they gave the landscape a new character.

The engineering of the railway also transformed the materials used in construction. Iron replaced wood and stone in many structures, and steel replaced iron in the later nineteenth century. The development of the Bessemer process, which allowed steel to be made cheaply in large quantities, made steel rails widely available by the 1870s, and steel rails were far more durable than iron ones. The rails were also heavier and more carefully designed, and they allowed locomotives and trains to become larger and more powerful. The railway was one of the largest consumers of steel in the late nineteenth century, and its demand helped to drive the growth of the steel industry.

The work of the navvies, the labourers who built the railways, was among the most physically demanding in the history of industry. Navvies dug cuttings, built embankments, laid track, and constructed bridges and tunnels, often under dangerous conditions and for low wages. They lived in makeshift camps, and their communities were often isolated and violent. The navvy was a figure of popular imagination, both admired for his strength and feared for his drunkenness and rowdiness. The railway could not have been built without the labour of these men, and their work is a fundamental part of its history.

# Electricity, Diesel, and the Reinvention of Traction

The steam locomotive dominated the railway for more than a century, but it was never the only possible form of traction, and it had serious limitations. Steam engines were inefficient, consuming large quantities of fuel and water, and they required extensive maintenance. They produced smoke and cinders, which polluted the air and created hazards in tunnels and in cities. They also required large depots and facilities for servicing, and their performance was limited by the difficulty of generating steam quickly and of controlling the fire. These problems encouraged engineers to look for alternatives, and by the end of the nineteenth century electric traction had become a serious possibility.

The electric railway was first demonstrated in Berlin in 1879, when the Siemens company exhibited a small electric locomotive at the Berlin Trades Exhibition. The locomotive drew current from a third rail and hauled a short train of carriages on a circular track. The demonstration was a sensation, and it showed that electric power could drive a railway vehicle reliably. Siemens went on to build the Gross-Lichterfelde tramway in Berlin, which opened in 1881 and was the first electric tramway in the world to carry passengers in regular service. Electric traction was soon adopted for urban and suburban railways, where its clean operation and quick acceleration were valuable.

The development of electric traction in Britain was led by inventors and engineers such as Magnus Volk, whose Volk's Electric Railway opened in Brighton in 1883 and is still operating today. The line ran along the seafront and was one of the first electric railways in Britain to carry passengers. Electric traction was also used on the first deep-level underground railway in London, the City and South London Railway, which opened in 1890 and used electric locomotives to haul its carriages through tunnels beneath the Thames. The line was a landmark in urban transport, and it showed that electric railways could operate underground without the smoke and steam that made steam traction impractical in tunnels.

The spread of electric traction was slowed by the difficulty of choosing a system of power supply. Direct current, which was used in the early systems, was simple and reliable, but it was difficult to transmit over long distances without large losses. Alternating current, which could be transformed to high voltages for efficient transmission, was more suitable for long-distance lines, but it was harder to use in traction motors. The competition between these systems, which had political and commercial dimensions as well as technical ones, shaped the development of electric railways for decades. The Valtellina line in Italy, electrified in 1902, used three-kilovolt direct current, and it was one of the first main-line electrifications in Europe.

The development of multiple-unit control, which allowed several self-propelled carriages to be operated from a single cab, was a major advance in electric railways. Frank Sprague, an American engineer, developed the system in the 1890s, and it was first used on the South Side Elevated Railway in Chicago in 1897. The system made it possible to run trains of varying lengths, and it greatly improved the efficiency of urban and suburban services. Multiple-unit control became standard on suburban railways throughout the world, and it remains the basis of much modern rail transport.

The electrification of main-line railways progressed slowly during the first half of the twentieth century. The Swiss railways adopted electric traction on a large scale, partly because of their dependence on hydroelectric power and their mountainous terrain, where electric locomotives had advantages over steam. The Swiss chose a single-phase alternating-current system at a low frequency, which made the locomotives simpler and the supply more efficient. Other countries, including France, Germany, and Sweden, electrified major lines and built electric locomotives for heavy freight and passenger traffic. In Britain, the Southern Railway and later British Railways electrified suburban lines around London and some main lines, but the bulk of the network remained steam-powered until the 1950s and 1960s.

The diesel engine offered another alternative to steam, and it became the dominant form of traction in many countries after the Second World War. The diesel engine, invented by Rudolf Diesel in the 1890s, was efficient and used cheap fuel, but it was heavy and difficult to adapt to the transmission of power to railway wheels. Early diesel locomotives used mechanical or hydraulic transmissions, which were unreliable, and the diesel-electric system, in which a diesel engine drove a generator that powered electric motors on the axles, proved to be the solution. The diesel-electric locomotive combined the flexibility of electric traction with the independence of an onboard power source.

The Burlington Zephyr, introduced in 1934 by the Chicago, Burlington and Quincy Railroad, was a streamlined, stainless-steel diesel-electric train that became a symbol of the modern railway. It was lightweight and fast, and it showed the potential of diesel traction for passenger services. The success of the Zephyr encouraged other railways to order diesel trains, and by the 1950s many American railways had replaced their steam locomotives with diesel-electric units. The General Motors Electro-Motive Division became one of the largest builders of diesel locomotives in the world, and its locomotives were used on railways in North America and elsewhere.

In Europe, the replacement of steam by diesel and electric traction was a longer and more uneven process. Germany, France, and Britain all made large investments in electrification and diesel traction in the decades after the Second World War, and the process was accelerated by the economic reconstruction of the 1950s. British Railways modernized its network with the Modernisation Plan of 1955, which committed the company to the replacement of steam by diesel and electric traction within a few years. The plan was ambitious, and it was only partly achieved, but it transformed the British railway, which was largely diesel-powered by the 1970s.

Diesel and electric traction changed the economics of the railway. They reduced the cost of fuel, cut the labour needed for maintenance and operation, and allowed trains to run more frequently and reliably. They also made it possible to run longer trains and to haul heavier loads, which improved the efficiency of freight transport. The railway became more competitive with road transport, which was growing rapidly in the same period, and this competition shaped the policy decisions of governments and railway companies.

The railway also changed in its architecture and its engineering. The locomotives and rolling stock of the mid-twentieth century were designed with new materials, such as welded steel and aluminium, and with new standards of comfort and reliability. The signalling systems were improved, with the introduction of automatic train control, track circuits, and electronic interlocking. The development of microelectronics in the later twentieth century added another layer of control, and the railway became one of the most technologically advanced industries of its time.

# The Race for Speed

Speed has always been a central preoccupation of the railway. The first locomotives moved at a walking pace, and the early railways were designed to carry goods and passengers at speeds that were far faster than the roads but that seem slow by later standards. The race for speed began in earnest in the mid-nineteenth century, when railway companies competed for passengers on the most lucrative routes, and it continued through the twentieth century, when speed became a symbol of national prestige and technological achievement.

The early railway speeds were modest by modern standards, but they were revolutionary in their time. Passengers on the Liverpool and Manchester in 1830 travelled at speeds of around thirty miles an hour in the best conditions, a pace that astonished contemporaries. The trains of the mid-nineteenth century ran at similar or somewhat higher speeds on the best lines, and the competition between railways led to increasing attention to the speed of express trains. The Great Western's broad-gauge trains, designed by Brunel and his locomotive engineers, were among the fastest in the world in the 1840s and 1850s, and their speed was one of the features that the Great Western advertised to passengers.

The London and Edinburgh route, which was the subject of intense competition between railway companies in the late nineteenth century, saw the first great races between trains. The so-called Races to the North in 1888 saw the rival companies compete to offer the fastest journey between London and Scotland, and the competition led to dangerous operating practices and to some remarkable feats of speed. The railway companies also built ever more powerful locomotives, and they experimented with larger driving wheels and higher boiler pressures, which made it possible to run trains at higher speeds with fewer stops.

The most famous steam speed record was set in 1938 by the British locomotive *Mallard*, designed by Nigel Gresley for the London and North Eastern Railway. On 3 July 1938, *Mallard* reached a speed of 126 miles per hour, or about 203 kilometres per hour, on a downhill stretch of track near Grantham. The record has never been broken by a steam locomotive, and it remains one of the most celebrated achievements in the history of the railway. The *Mallard* was a streamlined machine, designed to reduce air resistance and to allow the locomotive to run at high speed without excessive strain on its mechanism. Its record was set in a period of intense competition among railway companies and of growing public interest in speed and modernity.

The achievement of *Mallard* was followed by a long period in which the speed of the railway was limited by the technology of steam and by the state of the track. The development of electric and diesel traction, combined with improvements in track and signalling, allowed trains to run faster on main lines, but the most significant advances came after the Second World War, when governments began to invest in high-speed railways. The French and Japanese railways led the way, with projects that would transform the railway from a means of transport for the mass of travellers into a fast and reliable service that could compete with the airplane and the automobile.

In the twentieth century, the railway's speed records became a measure of national technological achievement. The French electric locomotives of the 1950s and 1960s set several speed records, and in 1955 a French electric locomotive reached a speed of more than 330 kilometres per hour on a test run. The record was later surpassed by high-speed trains designed for commercial service, and the race for speed moved from the locomotive to the train as a whole. The development of high-speed trains depended on advances in aerodynamics, materials science, traction motors, and control systems, and it reflected the growing sophistication of railway engineering.

Speed also raised questions about safety, environmental impact, and the cost of infrastructure. High-speed trains required new lines with gentle curves and gradients, and they could not run on the existing network without extensive modification. The construction of new lines was expensive, and it often involved the acquisition of land, the construction of tunnels and viaducts, and the management of environmental concerns. The engineering of high-speed lines therefore became a matter of intense debate, in which economic, political, and environmental considerations were weighed against the benefits of speed.

# High-Speed Rail: Japan, France, and After

The high-speed railway began in Japan. The Tōkaidō Shinkansen, which opened on 1 October 1964, connected Tokyo and Osaka, a distance of about 515 kilometres, in around four hours. It was built as a dedicated line with standard gauge, separate from the existing network, and it used a continuous welded track with gentle curves and gradients that allowed trains to run at speeds of up to 210 kilometres per hour at its opening. The line was built in time for the Tokyo Olympics of 1964, and it was a symbol of Japan's recovery from the Second World War and of its growing technological power. The Shinkansen was the first high-speed railway in the world, and its success transformed the expectations of travellers and of railway planners.

The Shinkansen was built by the Japanese National Railways, which was then a state-owned company with a large network of lines and a substantial labour force. The engineers of the company developed new trains and new track, and they drew on the experience of earlier Japanese railways and of the foreign railways they had studied. The trains were designed for high speed, with powerful electric motors, aerodynamic shapes, and sophisticated braking systems. The line was also designed to be highly reliable, with frequent services and a strict discipline of maintenance and operation. Its punctuality became famous, and its safety record was remarkable. The Shinkansen established a model that many other countries would later follow.

The Shinkansen network was extended over the following decades, with new lines to Sendai, Niigata, Hakodate, Kyushu, and other destinations. The network became a central part of Japan's transport system, and it changed the economy and society of the country. Businesses could operate across distances that had previously required a full day or more of travel, and regional cities gained access to the capital and to the markets of the wider country. The high-speed railway also reshaped the geography of Japan, encouraging the growth of some cities and the decline of others.

The French high-speed railway, the TGV, began service in 1981, when the first line from Paris to Lyon opened. The TGV was designed to run at speeds of up to 270 kilometres per hour on a dedicated line, and it used electric traction with a power supply of twenty-five kilovolts at fifty hertz. The TGV's success was remarkable, and it became the basis of a national network that linked Paris with the major cities of France and with neighbouring countries. The TGV was a symbol of French technological achievement, and it was promoted by the government as an instrument of regional development and national unity.

The TGV network was extended over the following decades, with lines to Lille, Strasbourg, Marseille, Bordeaux, and other cities, and with international connections to Belgium, Germany, Switzerland, Italy, Spain, and the United Kingdom. The system was built by a combination of state investment and private finance, and its operation was in the hands of the national railway company, the SNCF. The French high-speed railway was a model for other European countries, and its design influenced the development of the high-speed systems of Germany, Spain, and Italy.

Germany's high-speed service, the Intercity-Express or ICE, began operation in 1991, when the first lines between Hanover and Würzburg were opened. The German system was built partly on the existing network and partly on new lines, and it used both electric and diesel traction. The ICE was designed for speeds of up to 280 kilometres per hour, and it became the basis of a national network that connected the major cities of Germany and linked them with the rest of Europe. The reunification of Germany in 1990 gave the project additional urgency, since the eastern German railways needed to be modernized and integrated into the national network.

Italy's high-speed railway began with the Direttissima between Rome and Florence, which opened in 1977 and allowed trains to run at up to 250 kilometres per hour on a dedicated line. The Italian high-speed network was extended in the following decades, with new lines connecting Milan, Naples, Turin, and Venice. The Italian system was built partly by the state railway company, the Ferrovie dello Stato, and partly by private investors, and its growth was shaped by the political and economic conditions of the country.

Spain built its high-speed network in the early 1990s, with the line between Madrid and Seville opening in 1992 in time for the Seville Expo of that year. The Spanish system used the standard gauge for its high-speed lines, while its conventional network used the broader Iberian gauge, a difference that created problems for through services. The Spanish network was extended rapidly in the following decades, and by the twenty-first century it had become one of the largest high-speed systems in the world, connecting Madrid with Barcelona, Valencia, Málaga, and other cities.

The construction of high-speed rail in Britain was delayed by political and financial controversy, but the country eventually built the High Speed 1 line between London and the Channel Tunnel, which opened in stages between 2003 and 2007 and allowed Eurostar trains to run from London to Paris and Brussels at speeds of up to 300 kilometres per hour. The line was built as a new railway through the south-east of England, and it was financed partly by private investment. The British high-speed network was expanded in later years, but the plans for a larger network, known as High Speed 2, were controversial and were revised several times.

China's high-speed railway is the largest in the world. The first line, between Beijing and Tianjin, opened in August 2008, and it was followed by an enormous program of construction that created a network of more than forty thousand kilometres by the early 2020s. The Chinese system uses standard-gauge lines built to high standards, and its trains run at speeds of up to 350 kilometres per hour on the main lines. The Chinese network has transformed travel within the country, linking the major cities with frequent and reliable services, and it has been a major focus of Chinese industrial and infrastructure policy. The scale of the project has been widely noted, and its costs and benefits have been debated.

The development of high-speed rail in other parts of the world has been more uneven. Taiwan opened a high-speed line between Taipei and Kaohsiung in 2007. South Korea built a high-speed network, the KTX, beginning in 2004. Several other countries, including Turkey, Morocco, and Saudi Arabia, have built or are building high-speed lines. In the United States, high-speed rail has been proposed on several occasions, most notably in California, where a project to connect Los Angeles and San Francisco has been planned and partly built, but its completion has been slow and its costs have risen.

The technical foundations of high-speed rail rest on several elements. The track must be exceptionally smooth and stable, which requires precise construction and maintenance. The curves must be gentle, and the gradients must be shallow, which often requires new lines to be built rather than existing ones upgraded. The trains must be aerodynamic, with designs that reduce drag and noise, and they must be powered by electric motors that can deliver high power at high speed. The signalling systems must allow trains to run at close intervals with high safety, and they must be supported by sophisticated control systems. High-speed rail is therefore a system of systems, and its success depends on the coordination of many technical and organizational elements.

Magnetic levitation, or maglev, has been pursued as a more radical alternative to conventional high-speed rail. Maglev trains float above a guideway using magnetic forces, which removes the friction of wheels on rails and allows very high speeds. The German Transrapid system was tested extensively and was used for a commercial line in Shanghai, which opened in 2004 and connects the city with its international airport. The Shanghai line is about thirty kilometres long, and its trains reach speeds of up to 430 kilometres per hour. The Japanese SCMaglev has set speed records on test tracks, reaching more than 600 kilometres per hour in 2015, and it has been planned for a line between Tokyo and Nagoya, although its construction has been delayed. Maglev has remained a niche technology, limited by its cost and by the difficulty of integrating it with existing networks.

The speed record for conventional wheel-on-rail trains was set in 2007 by a French TGV running on a dedicated test line, which reached 574.8 kilometres per hour. The record was a demonstration of the capabilities of the technology, and it was achieved with a specially modified train. Commercial services operate at speeds well below the record, because the cost of wear, the consumption of energy, and the demands of safety and comfort make lower speeds more economical.

# Decline, Deregulation, and Renewal

The history of the railway in the twentieth century was not one of uninterrupted growth. In many countries, the railway faced decline in the decades after the Second World War, as road transport and air travel became cheaper and more convenient. Motor cars became affordable for the mass of people, and they offered a flexibility that the railway could not match. Trucks replaced the railway for much of the freight that had once been carried by train, and airlines took much of the long-distance passenger traffic that the railway had dominated. Many local lines were closed, and the network was reduced in size.

In Britain, the railway was nationalized in 1948, when the government created British Railways as a state-owned company that operated most of the country's lines. The nationalization was intended to modernize the railway and to remove the inefficiencies of a system that had been built by competing private companies. The nationalized railway faced serious problems, including the growing competition of road transport, the high cost of maintaining an aging network, and the difficulty of making the company profitable. The Beeching Report of 1963, written by Richard Beeching, recommended the closure of many branch lines and stations, and a large part of the network was closed over the following decade. The closures were controversial, and they remain a subject of debate.

The British railway was privatized in the 1990s, under a process that divided the network into many separate companies. The infrastructure was placed under a private company, Railtrack, which was later replaced by a public body, Network Rail. The trains were leased to private train operating companies that competed for franchises to run services. The privatization was a radical experiment, and its results were mixed. Some services improved, and passenger numbers grew, but the fragmentation of the system created problems of coordination, and the costs of the reform were high. The Hatfield rail crash of 2000 and the Potters Bar accident of 2002, among others, led to a reassessment of the management of the infrastructure and to the replacement of Railtrack.

Japan also went through a major reform of its railway. The Japanese National Railways was divided into several regional companies and a freight company in 1987, and these companies were privatized in the following years. The reform was intended to reduce the debts of the national railway, which had grown enormous, and to introduce competition and efficiency. The Japanese railway remained a national success, with high-speed trains, intensive urban services, and a reputation for punctuality and safety. The Japanese reform is often cited as a model of the restructuring of a national railway, and it showed that a privatized railway could maintain high standards of service.

The United States took a different path. Passenger rail service was in decline by the 1960s, and the government created the National Railroad Passenger Corporation, known as Amtrak, in 1971 to take over most of the country's intercity passenger services. Amtrak was a subsidized company, and its services were limited to a relatively small number of routes. The freight railroads were consolidated into a smaller number of large companies, and they became highly profitable in the later twentieth century, especially after the deregulation of rail freight by the Staggers Act of 1980. Freight railways in the United States now carry a large share of the country's goods over long distances, and they are among the most efficient rail systems in the world.

The freight railway was transformed by containerization. The standardized shipping container, developed in the 1950s and widely adopted from the 1960s, allowed goods to be moved between ships, trains, and trucks without being unloaded and reloaded. The container changed the economics of freight transport, and it made the railway more competitive with the truck and the ship. Container terminals and intermodal facilities became important parts of the railway network, and the railway's role in global supply chains grew.

Freight railways have also been shaped by heavy industries, such as coal, iron, steel, and minerals. The railway carried the coal that fuelled power stations and the iron ore that fed steelworks, and its fortunes were tied to the health of these industries. As the coal industry declined in many countries, the railway lost traffic, but it also gained new traffic from containers and from the movement of goods across continents. The railway remains a central part of the transport of bulk commodities, and it is among the most important carriers of coal, grain, and ore in the world.

Urban rail has also seen a revival in the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries. Light rail systems, metros, and commuter railways have been built in many cities, and they have been valued for their ability to carry large numbers of people with relatively little road space and with lower emissions than the private car. The metro systems of Paris, London, Tokyo, Moscow, and other cities are among the largest and most heavily used in the world, and new systems have been built in cities across Asia, the Middle East, and the Americas. The urban railway has become a symbol of modern urban planning, and its development has been linked to the growth of cities and to concerns about congestion and pollution.

The railway's relationship to the environment has become a central issue in the twenty-first century. Railways are generally more energy-efficient than road and air transport, and they produce lower emissions per passenger or tonne of freight.
